subject: Best way to compute log score in INLA ($marginals versus inla.posterior.sample)

messages.author: 7e30b96b125ca7f3
messages.subject: Best way to compute log score in INLA ($marginals versus inla.posterior.sample)
parts:
Hi all,
I'd like to evaluate the logarithmic score of a posterior marginal fitted using R-INLA (not leave-one-out cross-validation, it's simulated data so I have the true value) and am unsure about the best way to do it.

In the first approach, if the fitted model is called fit then I can access the (ith) posterior marginal using

df <- fit$marginals.fitted.values[[i]]

which gives a dataframe with $x and $y components. I can then use linear interpolation e.g. approxfun to create an approximate posterior which I can evaluate at the true value (and then take the logarithm). The problem with this is that sometimes I get -Inf logarithmic score because the truth evaluates to zero on the posterior (I'm running simulations so although this isn't common a single -Inf messes up the average). I think this could be because df doesn't have that many rows (as well I'm testing model mis-specfication so maybe some of the posteriors aren't that accurate so the truth is a bit further in the tail).

An alternative strategy would be to use kernel density estimation based upon samples drawn from the posterior marginal using inla.posterior.sample(n = big_number, fit, selection = list(Predictor = i)).

I'd be grateful for any guidance on this: Is there a way that I could increase the number of rows in the first approach? I assume that inla.posterior.sample is using more information about the posterior than is contained in df? Apologies if I've missed any obvious documentation on this.

Thanks,
Adam

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Best way to compute log score in INLA ($marginals versus inla.posterior.sample)
parts:
po=TRUE would only compute it for data used in the estimation, not for separate known validation data, so I don't think that would help in Adam's case.
I suspect the nicest method would be if there's a way to get inla to return the log of the marginal densities (which I think are already used internally; I recall some spline interpolation happening on the log-scale?)
and interpolation/evaluation could then be done on those.

However, Adam, you need to clarify if you need the log-marginal-densities of 1) the latent variables, 2) the linear predictor, 3) the transformed predictor (the "fitted values", which is a mis-naming from the literature since it is _not_ the distribution on the data scale, but just of the transformed linear predictor), or rather 4), the predictive log-density on the data scale (this would be what I would see as the log-score for validation data). For the latter, your best option is likely to use inla.posterior.sample(), since you can then add the data-level randomness on top of that as a postprocessing step of on the samples (or add it directly when using predict() or generate() in inlabru; I think there is now a way to do it also in inla, but I'm not familiar with the details for that).

Finn
